rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · Teaching Friday
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a sunlit clearing beside a timber fort, a bearded man in goatskin clothes teaching a young islander to speak new words and hold a bow, a parrot on a stake, two spears leaning on a tree, warm midday light, hopeful storybook illustration

blocks.text: Friday learned fast. In a few weeks he could talk with Robinson about almost anything under the sun. He learned the words for bread and milk, goat and corn, work and friend. He could joke now too, and his laugh could be heard all over the little fort. And he never once broke the promise he had made on the beach.
Friday learns new words, new work, and a new friend.

Robinson made Friday clothes of goatskin like his own, and gave him a hatchet to carry at his belt. Later he gave him a gun too, and taught him to shoot straight and far. Friday cooked the dinner, planted the seeds and milked the goats. And he asked a hundred questions about the great world beyond the sea.
New word: faithful — always loyal and true. Friday was faithful to Robinson all his life, in fair weather and in foul.

One evening, when the stars were coming out over the sea, Friday asked who made the sun and the stars and the water. Robinson told him about God, who made all things and loves all people. "Then He loves my people too," said Friday softly. Robinson took his hand and said that He did.

Together they sowed a bigger field of barley and rice than Robinson had ever managed alone. They reaped it, threshed it, and baked the finest bread that had ever come out of the island ovens. They fished in the bay, hunted goats on the hill, and talked from morning till night. The parrot Poll shrieked his name from the fence, and the two cats slept in the sun.

The island had been a lonely prison for many long years. Now, with Friday's laugh in it every day, it began to feel like home. Robinson did not know it yet, but the end of his long waiting was coming near.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Farm and the Fold
chapters.artPrompt: a strong ring of tall stakes around a shady hollow full of gentle milk-goats, a bearded man in goatskin milking one into a bowl, a young islander carrying hay, fields of golden corn beyond, a parrot on a fence rail, bright peaceful light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: With two pairs of hands the little farm grew quickly. They sowed more corn than Robinson had ever grown before, and the stalks stood tall and golden in the dry season. They dried grapes in the sun for raisins, and stored them in baskets in the cave, till there was food enough for years. Robinson had learned patience the hard way, and now patience paid him back.
The new goat fold in the shady wood, full of gentle milk-goats.

Then they built the fold. They caught young goats with snares and gentle hands, and penned them inside a strong ring of stakes in a shady hollow of the wood. Soon there were more than forty goats, so tame that they followed Friday about like a flock of dogs. Friday was wonderful with animals; even the wildest kid grew gentle in a week.

The goats gave rich milk, and Robinson learned to churn butter and press cheese — the first ever made on that island. There were eggs from wild hens, honey from hollow trees, and fish from the bay on calm days. Friday drank his milk warm and sweet, and said it was better than anything his own island ever grew.
New word: fold — a pen fenced all round, where animals are kept safe. Robinson's fold gave him milk, butter and cheese all year round.

When the rainy days came, they sat dry and warm inside the fort, mending nets and churning butter by the light of a candle of goat fat. The cave was full now: corn, raisins, rice, barrels of water and powder. It looked less like a cave than a little shop.

On Sundays they rested. Robinson read aloud from his great Bible, and Friday listened with his head on his knees, asking wise, simple questions. Work and prayer, bread and milk, and a friend to share it all — what more could anyone want? But the sea had one more story to tell.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Battle on the Shore
chapters.artPrompt: a tropical shore where two men stand back to back among palm trees with muskets raised, three large canoes on the sand, strangers running for the water, an old man kneeling free with ropes cut, stormy morning light, dramatic storybook illustration

blocks.text: One morning Friday came running, pale as ashes, with his spear in his hand. Boats were coming — three great canoes, full of strangers from a far island, bringing three poor prisoners with them. Friday knew too well what such visits meant. He shook with fear, and with anger too. The strangers were bigger and fiercer than any men Robinson had seen before.
Robinson and Friday stand together on the shore to save the prisoners.

Robinson gave Friday a musket, and kept one himself. They crept through the trees, low and quiet, until they could see the shore. Then they fired together, and the strangers scattered like birds — for they had never heard thunder come out of a man's hand before. Those who could run fled to their canoes and pushed off from the sand.

Two prisoners were left on the shore. One still lay bound by the fire, and Friday ran to cut his ropes — and gave a great cry, for the old man was his own father. The two of them laughed and wept and talked all at once. Friday brought him water and warm goats' milk, and for a long while he could not let go of his father's hand.
New word: prisoner — a person who is caught and held by others. Three prisoners had been brought to the island; three free men walked away from it.

The third prisoner had leapt into the sea when the shooting began, and lay half-drowned and hurt on the rocks. They carried him up to the fort and nursed him until he was strong again. He was a Spaniard, a kind and careful man, and Robinson was glad of every mouth to feed. He was no longer alone — and a new plan was growing in his mind.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Great Canoe
chapters.artPrompt: a huge dugout canoe lying in the shade of tall trees, a bearded man and a young islander scraping its hollowed hull, baskets of bread and barrels of water stacked beside it, a parrot shrieking from a branch above, dappled green light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The Spaniard told Robinson of sixteen of his countrymen, cast away like him on the mainland across the water. They were poor and patient, living on what the country gave, waiting for a rescue that never came. Robinson made a promise that very day. He would build them a boat, and the Spaniard and Friday's father would sail in it to bring them home.
The great canoe takes shape in the wood, big enough for them all.

They chose the tallest tree on the island and cut it down — it took twenty days of work. Then they hollowed it out with fire and adze, chopped and scraped and burned, until a great canoe lay in the shade. She was long enough to carry twenty men.

It was the biggest thing that had ever been built on the island, and they were proud of every plank of her. Even the parrot came to look, and shrieked "Robinson Crusoe!" from the branch above, as if he were blessing the work.

They loaded her with barrels of water, bags of rice, baskets of bread and raisins, and goats' milk in jars. When the high tide came they rolled her to the water on smooth logs, and she floated like a swan. The Spaniard and the old father stepped in with tears, blessed Robinson, and paddled away across the shining bay.
New word: tide — the slow rise and fall of the sea. They waited for the high tide to float the great canoe off the sand.

Then came the long waiting. The rainy season set in, and Robinson dug new cellars, made new barrels and planted a new field, while Friday watched the sea from the hill every day. They looked and looked for the boat to come back. It was a slow season of hope, and hope, Robinson found, is heavy to carry.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · An English Ship
chapters.artPrompt: an English sailing ship at anchor in a blue tropical bay at dusk, a small boat pulled up on the sand, three men with bound hands standing under palm trees, a bearded man in goatskin stepping out of the shadows, tense quiet light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Three years passed, and the boat did not come back. Then one morning Robinson woke to hear Friday shouting from the hill: a boat was on the water — a great boat, with an English ship lying at anchor in the bay! Robinson leaped up for joy. Then he stopped, and looked hard, and his heart went down again. It was the first English ship he had seen in twenty-eight years.
The castaway captain tells Robinson and Friday the tale of the mutiny.

For there was something wrong. The men in the boat were quarrelling like thieves, and when they came ashore they brought three prisoners with them, tied hand and foot. The prisoners were the ship's own captain, his honest mate, and a passenger. Their crew had risen against them in the night — a mutiny. The rebels meant to leave them on the island and sail away as pirates.
New word: crew — all the sailors who work on one ship. This crew had turned against their own captain and stolen his ship.

Robinson stepped out of the trees with Friday behind him, and asked the captain's story from beginning to end. When he had heard it all, he held out his hand. "Captain," he said, "help me and my man Friday, and I will help you to your ship again." The bearded stranger in goatskin clothes looked strange, but his eyes were steady, and the captain took the hand.

That night they counted the enemy. Ten rough sailors were ashore with muskets, and more lay asleep on the ship at anchor. Ten against four — but four who knew every path and cave on the island, and ten who knew nothing at all. Robinson smiled in the dark. He had lived with harder odds than that, for many years.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · Taking Back the Ship
chapters.artPrompt: mutineers kneeling on wet sand with muskets laid down, an honest sea captain standing over them, a bearded man in goatskin and a young islander with smoking muskets among palm trees, a ship's boat in the surf, early morning light, dramatic storybook illustration

blocks.text: The plan began well, for luck was with them. Two sailors who had never loved the mutiny came wandering into the wood, and Robinson's little band stepped out and took their muskets before they could cry out. Both men were treated kindly, and both swore on the spot to be true to their captain again. So the band grew from four to six, and every man of it was eager.
The mutineers kneel on the sand and beg their captain for mercy.

The rest of the rebels lay round their fire in the dark, singing and drinking, with their muskets stacked. The captain crept near with Robinson and Friday, and at a word the guns spoke together. The loudest rebel fell, and the rest tumbled up from the grass, threw down their arms and begged for mercy. "Well done, Friday!" cried Robinson, as one rebel after another gave in.

"You shall have mercy," said Robinson. "But the two worst of you shall stay behind on this island, with food and tools and powder. Here you shall learn what patience can teach." The two ringleaders knelt and wept, for they knew they deserved far worse. Robinson promised to tell them how to live, for he had been a castaway once himself. The rest climbed into the boat, shouting like schoolboys let out of school.
New word: mercy — kindness shown to someone who has done wrong. The rebels begged for mercy, and mercy was what they got.

Then Robinson and Friday rowed out with the captain to the English ship at anchor in the bay. When the honest sailors on deck saw their true captain stand at the rail again, they gave three great cheers that rang across the water. The mutiny was over, and the ship was his once more.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Voyage Home
chapters.artPrompt: a tall English sailing ship running before the wind on a wide blue sea, a bearded man in a fine new coat and a goatskin cap at the rail, a young islander pointing at the great sails, a parrot on his shoulder, an island sinking far behind, bright hopeful light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: On a clear morning in December, in the year 1686, Robinson Crusoe stepped aboard the English ship. He had lived on his island for twenty-eight years, two months and nineteen days. He carried little away with him: his goatskin cap, his great umbrella, his parrot Poll, and the money that had lain useless in the cave for all those years. How small it all looked in his hands.
The ship stands out to sea, and the island sinks slowly behind.

Friday went with him, wide-eyed at the towering masts and the great white sails. "Master! Master!" cried Friday, pointing at everything at once. The captain shook Robinson's hand and called him the bravest man he had ever met. Then the anchor came up, the sails filled with wind, and the island that had been a prison and then a home sank quietly into the sea.

It was a long voyage home, over seas Robinson had sailed as a young fool. At last he saw England again — older, wiser, and rich too. The plantation he had left behind in Brazil had grown and grown while he was away, and the money had been kept safe for him. He was nearly sixty, but he stood as straight as any man on the quay.
New word: plantation — a great farm far away, worked for its owner. Robinson's plantation in Brazil had made him rich without his knowing it.

Robinson married, and had children of his own, and told them the story of the island till their eyes grew round. And in later years, when the sea called him again, he sailed back to visit it once more. He went to see the fort on the hill, the fold in the wood, and the brave men he had left to keep it.
